title: Leadership development
note: These are preferences: the parts of leading you enjoy most and least today. They are not abilities, they change with experience, and they must never be used to select, promote or rate anyone.

strategic.short: Looking ahead and connecting today's work to a longer-term direction.
strategic.preferred: You may naturally help a team see why its work matters and where it is heading.
strategic.stretch: Setting aside regular time to look further ahead could help you lead beyond the next deadline.

collaborative.short: Shaping plans and decisions together with the people involved.
collaborative.preferred: You may build commitment by involving people early and sharing ownership.
collaborative.stretch: Inviting others into a decision before it is made could strengthen buy-in and ideas.

coaching.short: Helping people grow by asking, listening and supporting stretch.
coaching.preferred: You may enjoy helping others find their own answers and grow in confidence.
coaching.stretch: Swapping one piece of advice for one good question could help others grow faster.

delegating.short: Handing over real ownership, not just tasks.
delegating.preferred: You may free up your time and build trust by letting others own outcomes.
delegating.stretch: Handing over one whole piece of work, including its decisions, could build trust both ways.

deciding.short: Making and explaining choices, especially under uncertainty.
deciding.preferred: You may help a team move forward by making clear, explained calls.
deciding.stretch: Agreeing how and when a decision will be made could help you decide with more confidence.

communicating.short: Keeping people informed and checking understanding.
communicating.preferred: You may keep people aligned by sharing information early and clearly.
communicating.stretch: A short, regular update rhythm could save confusion and repeated questions.

conflict.short: Raising and working through disagreement constructively.
conflict.preferred: You may help a team deal with tension early, before it grows.
conflict.stretch: Practising how to open a difficult conversation could make the next one easier.

team_development.short: Building how a team works together and learns.
team_development.preferred: You may enjoy shaping a team's habits, welcome and ways of learning.
team_development.stretch: A short team check-in on how you work together could surface easy improvements.

planning.short: Turning goals into plans, owners and dates, and keeping them on track.
planning.preferred: You may give a team clarity about who does what and by when.
planning.stretch: Writing down milestones and owners for one goal could make progress easier to see.

modules.title: Setting direction
modules.summary: Connect everyday work to a direction people can describe in their own words.

lessons.title: Purpose before plans
lessons.text: People commit more readily when they understand why the work matters. Before talking about tasks, explain the problem you are solving and who it helps.

lessons.title: Look up and ahead
lessons.text: Direction rarely appears in a busy week. A short, regular slot for thinking about trends, risks and opportunities keeps you from leading only the next deadline.

activities.title: Write the one-sentence direction
steps: Write one sentence about where your team or project should be in a year.
Ask two people to describe the direction in their own words.
Note any differences and adjust how you explain it.

activities.title: Book a thinking slot
steps: Block 30 minutes in your calendar each week for the next month.
Use it to list one trend, one risk and one opportunity.
Share one idea with your team afterwards.

modules.reflection: Which part of your work would people struggle to connect to a bigger purpose today?

modules.title: Deciding together
modules.summary: Involve people in the right decisions, at the right time, in the right way.

lessons.title: Say how a decision will be made
lessons.text: Collaboration goes wrong when people think they are deciding but are only being consulted. Say up front whether you will decide, decide after input, or let the group decide.

lessons.title: Ask before you anchor
lessons.text: Once a leader shares a preferred answer, others tend to follow it. Ask for ideas first, then share your own.

activities.title: Name the decision mode
steps: Pick an upcoming decision.
Tell the people involved whether you will decide, decide after input, or let them decide.
Afterwards, ask whether that felt clear and fair.

activities.title: Ideas first, mine last
steps: In your next planning conversation, ask everyone for an idea before giving yours.
Write all ideas down without judging them.
Notice whether any idea was better than your own starting point.

modules.reflection: When did you last change your mind because of someone else's idea?

modules.title: Coaching conversations
modules.summary: Help people find their own answers and grow through stretch.

lessons.title: Questions before advice
lessons.text: Advice solves today's problem; good questions build someone's ability to solve the next one. Try asking what they have already considered and what they would try first.

lessons.title: Stretch with support
lessons.text: People grow most from work slightly beyond their current comfort, with a clear way to ask for help. Agree on check-in points rather than stepping in.

activities.title: Three questions
steps: Next time someone brings you a problem, ask: what have you tried, what options do you see, and what would you do?
Only offer your view after those three questions.
Note how the conversation changed.

activities.title: Offer one stretch task
steps: Choose a task slightly beyond someone's current experience.
Agree on what success looks like and when you will check in.
Afterwards, ask what they learned and what support helped.

modules.reflection: Whose growth would benefit most from a coaching conversation this month?

modules.title: Delegating well
modules.summary: Hand over ownership, not just tasks, and agree how you will stay in touch.

lessons.title: Delegate outcomes
lessons.text: Delegating a list of steps keeps you as the bottleneck. Delegate the result you need, the limits that apply, and the decisions the person can make on their own.

lessons.title: Agree the check-ins
lessons.text: Hovering and disappearing both undermine delegation. Agree in advance when and how you will check progress.

activities.title: Hand over one whole piece of work
steps: Pick one piece of work you usually keep.
Explain the outcome, the limits and the decisions they own.
Agree two check-in points and stick to them.

activities.title: Match work to strengths
steps: List the main tasks coming up.
Ask each person which task they would most like to own and why.
Use their answers when you next assign work.

modules.reflection: What do you keep doing yourself that someone else could own?

modules.title: Making clear decisions
modules.summary: Decide with enough information, explain the reasons, and review the outcome.

lessons.title: Good enough to decide
lessons.text: Waiting for complete information often costs more than a reversible decision. Ask whether a decision is easy or hard to undo, and match your care to that.

lessons.title: Explain the why
lessons.text: People accept decisions they disagree with more readily when they understand the reasons and the options that were weighed.

activities.title: Sort decisions by reversibility
steps: List three decisions you are putting off.
Mark each one as easy or hard to undo.
Make one easy-to-undo decision this week.

activities.title: Write a short decision note
steps: For your next decision, write the options, what mattered most and why you chose.
Share it with the people affected.
Review the note a month later: what would you do differently?

modules.reflection: Which decision are you delaying, and what would make it easier to take?

modules.title: Communicating clearly
modules.summary: Share information early, keep a rhythm, and check understanding.

lessons.title: Before they have to ask
lessons.text: When people have to chase information, trust drops. A predictable rhythm of short updates prevents most surprises.

lessons.title: Check what landed
lessons.text: What you said and what people heard can differ. Ask people to play back the key points in their own words.

activities.title: Start a weekly three-line update
steps: Each week, share what changed, what is next and where you need help.
Keep it to three lines.
After a month, ask whether it helps.

activities.title: Ask for a play-back
steps: After explaining something important, ask someone to summarise it.
Fill any gaps without blame.
Notice which parts were most often misheard.

modules.reflection: What do people on your team most often learn too late?

modules.title: Working through conflict
modules.summary: Raise issues early and help people with different views move forward.

lessons.title: Early and specific
lessons.text: Small issues are easier to discuss than big ones. Describe what happened and its effect, without labelling the person.

lessons.title: Interests behind positions
lessons.text: Two people arguing for different solutions often want compatible things underneath. Ask each what they need and why.

activities.title: Prepare an opening line
steps: Think of an issue you have been avoiding.
Write one sentence that describes what happened and its effect, without blame.
Use it in a conversation this week.

activities.title: Map the needs
steps: When two views clash, ask each person what they need from the outcome.
Write the needs side by side.
Look for an option that meets the most important need on each side.

modules.reflection: Which disagreement would be easier to solve if it had been raised a month ago?

modules.title: Building team habits
modules.summary: Agree how the team works together and keep learning from experience.

lessons.title: Make the unwritten rules visible
lessons.text: Every team has habits about meetings, replies and decisions. Writing a few down helps new people settle in and surfaces disagreements early.

lessons.title: Learn on purpose
lessons.text: Teams improve fastest when they regularly ask what went well and what to change, and then actually change one thing.

activities.title: Draft a working agreement
steps: Ask the team for three habits that help them work well together.
Write them down and share them.
Revisit them after a month.

activities.title: Run a 15-minute retrospective
steps: Ask: what went well, what was hard, what will we change?
Pick one change and an owner.
Check on it at the next retrospective.

modules.reflection: What would a new team member find confusing about how your team works?

modules.title: Plans that work
modules.summary: Turn goals into milestones, owners and dates, and adjust as things change.

lessons.title: Milestones and owners
lessons.text: A goal without milestones and owners is a wish. Break it into steps that each have one owner and a date.

lessons.title: Plans are for changing
lessons.text: A plan is a tool for noticing change early, not a promise. Review it regularly and adjust openly.

activities.title: Map one goal
steps: Choose one goal for the next three months.
Write three to five milestones, each with one owner and a date.
Share it and invite corrections.

activities.title: Hold a short plan review
steps: Every two weeks, compare progress with the plan.
Agree what to change, drop or add.
Tell the people affected what changed and why.

modules.reflection: Which goal would benefit most from clearer owners and dates?
